To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have developed and evaluated the first paper-based, micro-fluidic fingerstick test, which is capable of rapid, semi- quantitative, visual measurement of ALT.

we have performed the field evaluation of a prototype paper-based, micro-fluidic fingerstick test to measure blood alanine amino-transferase (ALT) in HIV patients, which demonstrated high inter-operator reproducibility, low invalid rate, and acceptable accuracy.
a paper-based, point-of-care fingerstick test for alanine aminatransferase (a biomarker of drug-induced liver injury) has high inter-operator agreement and accuracy in a field setting.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a point-of-care test for liver injury, which is an important cause of death in the developing world.
the development of a low cost, point-of-care (PoC) diagnostic for monitoring drug-induced liver injury.
developing and evaluating a paper-based microfluidics device for rapid, visual detection of liver damage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the field evaluation of the paper-based ALT assay was successful, demonstrating that the device is feasible for use in a clinical setting, with the caveat that the device requires further optimization and quality control to ensure accurate results.
the paper based microfluidic finger-stick device is a feasible platform for POC ALT testing, but that further optimization and testing is required before it is ready for widespread clinical use.

the paper-based fingerstick ALT test has demonstrated high inter-operator reproducibility, low lot variability, low device failure rate, acceptable accuracy, and operational feasibility, and thus is a promising prototype for further field testing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the field evaluation of a prototype paper-based point-of-care transaminase test was successful.

the paper-based ALT device has been shown to be feasible for field evaluation, and that the results obtained from this evaluation can be used to inform further design and development of this and similar devices.

this paper based device has the potential to be a useful tool for the clinical management of patients with HIV in resource-limited countries, and could be a useful tool in the future to help identify patients at risk for drug induced liver injury (DIL) in these populations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a prototype fingerstick test for ALT is feasible, reproducible, and accurate enough for further field testing and eventual clinical deployment in resource-limited countries.
a paper-based microfluidics platform for rapid, semi quantitative, visual measurement of ALT is feasible and can be optimized for use in resource-limited clinical settings.
the device can be successfully deployed in a target setting by local personnel, and can be improved to achieve high accuracy and reliability.
